content.title: Best Editing Nominees at the 2026 Oscars, Ranked
content.text: Image via Apple Original Films Published Mar 13, 2026, 2:39 PM EDT Ross Bonaime is the Senior Film Editor at Collider. He is a Virginia-based critic, writer, and editor who has written about all forms of entertainment for Paste Magazine, Brightest Young Things, Flickchart, The Free Lance-Star, and more. Ross graduated from George Mason University with a focus in communications and journalism and a minor in film and video studies. Ross is a Tomatometer-approved critic, a member of the Washington DC Area Film Critics Association, and a member of the Critics Choice Association. He has loved movies ever since he saw Cinderella in the theater as a kid, he can quote 10 Things I Hate About You and Wet Hot American Summer from memory, and is fascinated by all things Georges Méliès and Charlie Chaplin. Sign in to your Collider account So many filmmakers say that editing is the final step of the storytelling process when it comes to a film. The first is the screenplay, the second is the directing of the project, but in the editing room, that's where the story truly comes together. Editors help pick the right takes, the right cuts, and the right order to truly heighten a story to be the best it can be. This year at the Oscars, we have five nominees who prove that to be the truth, in everything from a racing film, a horror story, a family drama, an ambitious sports tale, and an adventure to bring a family back together. This year's films featured some incredible editing, so let's take a look at this year's nominees in Best Editing. 5 'Marty Supreme' - Ronald Bronstein and Josh Safdie Image via A24 It makes perfect sense that Marty Supreme screenwriters Ronald Bronstein and Josh Safdie also edited this story of an ambitious table tennis player. This film needs to move with a frenetic energy, always moving forward without ever slowing down, and keeping its audience on the edge of their seats. They know where the beats are and how to keep this story propelled until the final shots, and that likely makes them the best men to edit this bonkers story. It also probably doesn’t hurt that, since Bronstein and Safdie have written together now for two decades, with films like Heaven Knows What, Good Time, and Uncut Gems, they know exactly what each other wants. 4 'Sinners' - Michael P. Shawver Image via © Warner Bros. / Courtesy Everett Collection But Shawver's work becomes even more impressive after reading Coogler's script for Sinners and seeing how Shawver has reorganized the story to give it even more power. For example, Coogler's screenplay begins with Jack O'Connell's Remmick introducing himself at the home of the Klan members before turning them into vampires. Instead, Sinnerssaves that for much later, which makes its sudden impact even stronger. It's also fantastic how Shawver will cut back to earlier moments during sequences of great emotional depth, which escalates the audience's feelings in surprising ways — like when he cuts to Delroy Lindo's Delta Slim giving Miles Caton's Sammie advice before we cut to the "I Lied to You" sequence, or seeing moments between Michael B. Jordan's Smoke and Stack after Stack has passed. It's little touches like this that make Sinners even richer than it already was. 3 'Sentimental Value' - Olivier Bugge Coutté Editor Olivier Bugge Coutté has worked with writer-director Joachim Trier ever since he was making shorts in the late ‘90s and early 2000’s, all the way to Trier’s features, and it’s very clear that Coutté knows just the right way to piece together Trier’s often fractured narratives. But with Sentimental Value, Trier has made maybe his most ambitious film yet, one that follows a century of one family and their time in their Oslo home. Sentimental Value jumps back and forth through time liberally, changes perspectives multiple times, and even tries to trick us into thinking moments of movies being filmed are actually reality. It’s a lot to maintain in one film, but Coutté makes it look effortless. 2 'F1' - Stephen Mirrione Image via Apple Original Films F1 might be Mirrione’s grandest piece of work, an intense racing film that spans the globe and multiple high-octane races. A great racing film is often made by its editing, and Mirrione makes us feel every twist and turn on the road, puts us right down with the racers, and often shows us these races from the perspective of two different competitors. From a technical level, it’s truly bonkers what both director Joseph Kosinski and Mirrione are doing here, and it certainly puts F1 in the running as one of the all-time great racing films. The voters love a big, bombastic, and impressive editing job in this category, and that could very well mean F1 earns Mirrione his second Oscar. 1 'One Battle After Another' - Andy Jurgensen Image via Warner Bros.
